power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Thirty-six participants (18 dyads of strangers matched by sex assigned at birth; 9 female pairs and 9 male pairs) participated in the study. Two dyads were excluded from further analysis due to technical issues during the recording session. Since no previous quantitative research had examined the physiological effects of biosignal sharing in social interaction, we conducted a power analysis based on the presumably smaller contrast of interest in our study, that is, for a paired-samples t-test between the two levels of biosignal sharing. We targeted a medium-to-large effect size (d = 0.50) with a significance threshold of 0.05. The result indicated that 34 participants would provide an 80% chance of detecting the effect of interest.

text.text: Advances in digital technology have made physiological signals such as electrocardiography (ECG) and electrodermal activity (EDA) increasingly accessible, enabling previously covert bodily states to be shared in real time during social exchanges.
Recent work, primarily qualitative, suggests that biosignal sharing can modulate social interaction, yet quantitative evidence on its psychophysiological impact remains limited.
Here, we investigated whether biosignal sharing during social interaction, and in particular the reciprocity of such information exchange, modulates psychophysiological responses.
We present data from 18 sex-matched dyads (N = 36) of strangers, whose ECG and EDA were recorded while they engaged in nonverbal face-to-face interaction.
Participants shared their heart rate and skin conductance levels (displayed on a monitor) either unidirectionally, bidirectionally, or not at all.

We examined the effects of biosignal sharing on indices of autonomic nervous system activity (including RMSSD, skin conductance level, and the number and amplitude of skin conductance responses) and related these measures to psychometric assessments of empathic traits, social interaction anxiety, perceived scrutiny, and interpersonal closeness.

Bidirectional biosignal sharing significantly reduced both the skin conductance level and the number of skin conductance responses compared to both face-toface interaction without sharing and unidirectional sharing.
Moreover, greater reductions in sympathetic activation during bidirectional sharing were associated with larger increases in perceived interpersonal closeness.
Correlational analyses further indicated that the perceived scrutiny was linked to heightened arousal and reduced closeness.
Our findings advance the understanding of the psychophysiological impact of biosignal sharing, with direct implications for the design of social computing systems and computer-mediated interaction.
Human social interaction relies not only on what people say or do, but also on subtle physiological responses that signal emotional and cognitive states.
Mind and body are deeply intertwined and mutually influence one another (Cacioppo et al., 2007; Critchley, 2009; Hugdahl, 1995).

text.text: Physiological measures such as electrocardiography (ECG) and electrodermal activity (EDA) provide non-invasive windows into these dynamics, reflecting the regulation of the parasympathetic and sympathetic branches of the ANS (Boucsein, 2012; Dawson et al., 2017; Levinson and Hajcak, 2020; Shaffer and Ginsberg, 2017; Thayer and Lane, 2000).

text.text: Together, these biosignals offer insights not only into intra-individual bodily states (ECG: Arakaki et al., 2023; Balzarotti et al., 2017; Gullett et al., 2023; EDA: Boucsein, 2012; Levinson and Hajcak, 2020) but also into how psychophysiological processes are shaped by, and informative for, social interaction (Candini et al., 2021; Deits-Lebehn et al., 2023; Helminen et al., 2011; Jauniaux et al., 2020; Mauersberger et al., 2022; Myllyneva and Hietanen, 2015; Palumbo et al., 2017; Petrocchi and Cheli, 2019; Prochazkova et al., 2022; Quintana et al., 2012; Sariñana-González et al., 2017; Thayer and Lane, 2000), including technologically mediated exchanges (Ekman et al., 2012; Järvelä et al., 2014; Perugia et al., 2017; Torres et al., 2024).

text.text: In everyday social interactions, we rely on overt cues, such as blushing, tone of voice, or body language, to infer others' emotional and mental states.
If made accessible, covert bodily signals may also carry valuable information about these states and shape social interaction.

Recent research has therefore moved from treating biosignals merely as internal markers of psychophysiological states to exploring how externalizing them can provide socially meaningful cues (Chanel and Mühl, 2015; Feijt et al., 2023; Moge et al., 2022; Stepanova et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Recent research has therefore moved from treating biosignals merely as internal markers of psychophysiological states to exploring how externalizing them can provide socially meaningful cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chanel and Mühl, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Feijt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Moge et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Stepanova et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Biosignal sharing refers to the practice of making covert physiological signals (e.g., ECG, EDA) overtly available to others.

While such information has traditionally been used intrapersonally for self-regulation (e.g., biofeedback), current work in affective computing and human-computer interaction (HCI) highlights the interpersonal potential of these signals in shaping social interaction (Chanel and Mühl, 2015; Janssen, 2012; Moge et al., 2022).
text.formatted: While such information has traditionally been used intrapersonally for self-regulation (e.g., biofeedback), current work in affective computing and human-computer interaction (HCI) highlights the interpersonal potential of these signals in shaping social interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chanel and Mühl, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Janssen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Moge et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Comprehensive reviews em-phasize that biosignal sharing may support communication, increase awareness of others' emotions, and foster social connection, while also underscoring the importance of design choices (including how and to whom this information is disclosed) in shaping these effects (Feijt et al., 2023; Stepanova et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Comprehensive reviews em-phasize that biosignal sharing may support communication, increase awareness of others' emotions, and foster social connection, while also underscoring the importance of design choices (including how and to whom this information is disclosed) in shaping these effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Feijt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Stepanova et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A growing body of qualitative and design-oriented studies illustrates how biosignal sharing can shape social interaction across several domains.
First, shared biosignals can influence how people interpret affect and emotion.

For example, heart-rate visualizations in chat or mobile interfaces have encouraged partners to better recognize each other's feelings and promoted empathy and attentiveness (Hassib et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For example, heart-rate visualizations in chat or mobile interfaces have encouraged partners to better recognize each other's feelings and promoted empathy and attentiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hassib et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Liu et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Even imagined scenarios involving shared heart-rate information have been shown to influence judgments of trust and cooperation (Merrill and Cheshire, 2017).
text.formatted: Even imagined scenarios involving shared heart-rate information have been shown to influence judgments of trust and cooperation <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Merrill and Cheshire, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, color-changing garments linked to skin conductance prompted friends to validate emotions, signal engagement, or reflect more deeply on their affective states (Howell et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Similarly, color-changing garments linked to skin conductance prompted friends to validate emotions, signal engagement, or reflect more deeply on their affective states <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Howell et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Second, biosignals can cue presence, intimacy, and connectedness.

Romantic couples reported greater closeness when sharing their heart rates (Slovák et al., 2012a (Slovák et al., , 2012b)), and workplace employees described a stronger sense of human contact when heart rate was displayed during collaboration (Wikström et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Romantic couples reported greater closeness when sharing their heart rates <ref type="bibr">(Slovák et al., 2012a</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Slovák et al., , 2012b))</ref>, and workplace employees described a stronger sense of human contact when heart rate was displayed during collaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Wikström et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Along similar lines, sharing breathing patterns through virtual reality installations or vibrotactile displays enhanced feelings of connection with others and with nature (El Ali et al., 2023; Stepanova et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Along similar lines, sharing breathing patterns through virtual reality installations or vibrotactile displays enhanced feelings of connection with others and with nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(El Ali et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Stepanova et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, biosignal sharing has been explored as a means to support collaboration and performance.

In problem-solving tasks, providing multimodal biofeedback of heart rate, electrodermal activity, and respiration reduced stress and workload while improving clarity of communication (Tan et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In problem-solving tasks, providing multimodal biofeedback of heart rate, electrodermal activity, and respiration reduced stress and workload while improving clarity of communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Tan et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that biosignals can function as socially meaningful cues and that they have value in supporting joint action and computer-mediated interactions.
Alongside these promising findings, research also highlights that the effects of biosignal sharing are often ambiguous and context-dependent.

Access to heart-rate information, for example, can lead to divergent social evaluations depending on situational framing: elevated heart rate may be interpreted as anxiety during interpersonal conflict, whereas a lack of elevation may be perceived as indifference e.g. when arriving late to a meeting (Merrill and Cheshire, 2016).
text.formatted: Access to heart-rate information, for example, can lead to divergent social evaluations depending on situational framing: elevated heart rate may be interpreted as anxiety during interpersonal conflict, whereas a lack of elevation may be perceived as indifference e.g. when arriving late to a meeting <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Merrill and Cheshire, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: People may also learn to attribute meaning to artificial physiological signals, creating new but potentially misleading social mappings (Merrill and Cheshire, 2017).
text.formatted: People may also learn to attribute meaning to artificial physiological signals, creating new but potentially misleading social mappings <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Merrill and Cheshire, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Similar ambiguities have been reported for socially shared EDA, where participants struggled to interpret feedback consistently and employed it in divergent ways (Howell et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Similar ambiguities have been reported for socially shared EDA, where participants struggled to interpret feedback consistently and employed it in divergent ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Howell et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, willingness to share biosignals depends strongly on context.

Participants tend to feel more comfortable sharing physiological signals in playful or positive settings, such as gaming, than in professional or adversarial ones (Buschek et al., 2018; Hassib et al., 2017; Slovák et al., 2012b).
text.formatted: Participants tend to feel more comfortable sharing physiological signals in playful or positive settings, such as gaming, than in professional or adversarial ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Buschek et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hassib et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Slovák et al., 2012b)</ref>.

text.text: In workplace studies, heart-rate sharing increased feelings of human contact but also raised concerns about intimacy, professionalism, and work efficiency (Wikström et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In workplace studies, heart-rate sharing increased feelings of human contact but also raised concerns about intimacy, professionalism, and work efficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Wikström et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These concerns often center on privacy and impression management: since physiological signals are involuntary and difficult to control, sharing them can feel like a loss of autonomy over what is revealed about one's internal states and how one is perceived by others (Feijt et al., 2023; Slovák et al., 2012b).
text.formatted: These concerns often center on privacy and impression management: since physiological signals are involuntary and difficult to control, sharing them can feel like a loss of autonomy over what is revealed about one's internal states and how one is perceived by others <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Feijt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Slovák et al., 2012b)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, design features of biosignal-sharing systems appear to shape how such concerns are experienced.
For instance, the degree of reciprocity in the exchange may modulate both perceived risks and potential benefits.

Bidirectional sharing, in which interaction partners mutually disclose their biosignals, has been suggested to promote intimacy and trust while mitigating privacy concerns, whereas unidirectional setups may heighten feelings of exposure and social evaluation (Feijt et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Bidirectional sharing, in which interaction partners mutually disclose their biosignals, has been suggested to promote intimacy and trust while mitigating privacy concerns, whereas unidirectional setups may heighten feelings of exposure and social evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Feijt et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the centrality of reciprocity in many proposed applications of biosignal sharing, its role in shaping psychophysiological and interpersonal outcomes has received limited systematic investigation.
Overall, biosignals hold strong social meaning, and sharing them during social interaction has shown broad potential to shape subjective experiences and interpersonal dynamics.
Yet, despite this growing body of work, most existing studies remain qualitative or design-oriented (Feijt et al., 2023; Stepanova et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Yet, despite this growing body of work, most existing studies remain qualitative or design-oriented <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Feijt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Stepanova et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, there is a clear need for quantitative, controlled investigations to determine how biosignal sharing influences both social behavior and psychophysiological states.
We addressed three central questions: (1) Does biosignal sharing during social interaction influence individuals' psychophysiological states?
(2) Does the reciprocity of information exchange modulate these effects?
(3) How do individual psychological traits shape these responses?

To this end, we conducted an experiment in which pairs of strangers engaged in face-to-face interactions while their electrocardiography (ECG) and electrodermal activity (EDA) were simultaneously recorded.
We implemented a setup that displayed participants' ECG, heart rate (HR), and EDA in real time on a monitor visible to their partner.

The study design included three levels of sharing: (1) Face-to-face (no sharing), (2) Unidirectional sharing (one participant shares while the other observes), and (3) Bidirectional sharing (mutual simultaneous sharing).

We examined the effects of these conditions on indices of autonomic activity and their relationship to in-dividual differences in empathy and social anxiety, and to changes in perceived interpersonal closeness.
>Materials and methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Materials and methods</head>

text.text: Thirty-six participants (18 dyads of strangers matched by sex assigned at birth; 9 female pairs and 9 male pairs) participated in the study.
Two dyads were excluded from further analysis due to technical issues during the recording session.

Since no previous quantitative research had examined the physiological effects of biosignal sharing in social interaction, we conducted a power analysis based on the presumably smaller contrast of interest in our study, that is, for a paired-samples t-test between the two levels of biosignal sharing.
We targeted a medium-to-large effect size (d = 0.50) with a significance threshold of 0.05.
The result indicated that 34 participants would provide an 80% chance of detecting the effect of interest.
The participants were mainly students or researchers in the Helsinki area, aged 18-30 years (females: mean (M) age ± standard deviation (SD): 24.75 ± 3.72 years; males: 24.69 ± 3.39 years).

Eligibility criteria included a good understanding of spoken English, no diagnosed psychiatric, neurological, or cardiovascular disorders, and no use of drugs or treatments affecting the central nervous system (CNS) or cardiac activity.
Participants were also provided with a set of behavioral recommendations to follow 2 to 3 hours before the experiment to optimize data quality (Quintana and Heathers, 2014).
text.formatted: Participants were also provided with a set of behavioral recommendations to follow 2 to 3 hours before the experiment to optimize data quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Quintana and Heathers, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: These recommendations included avoiding nicotine, caffeine, and vigorous activity, as well as staying hydrated and sated while avoiding overeating and excessive water consumption.
All participants provided written, informed consent prior to the study.
As compensation, they received a lunch voucher with an approximate value of €13.
The experimental sessions were conducted at the Aalto Behavioral Laboratory (ABL) at Aalto University.
The study was approved by the Aalto University Research Ethics Committee (reference: D/1339/03.04/2023).

The experiment consisted of four face-to-face conditions differing in the level and reciprocity of biosignal sharing: (i) face-to-face interaction without biosignal sharing (F2F), (ii) unidirectional biosignal sharing in which one participant shared their biosignals while being observed (Sharing; S), (iii) the complementary role in which the participant observed the partner's biosignals without sharing (Observing; O), and (iv) bidirectional biosignal sharing (BS), in which both participants shared and observed each other's biosignals simultaneously (see Figure 1).

text.text: Each experimental condition lasted 5 min and was preceded by a baseline period during which participants watched an emotionally neutral video (Jennings et al., 1992), which lasted approximately 4 min and featured relaxing scenes of fish and coral reefs.

text.text: The order of the experimental conditions was counterbalanced across dyads to control for order effects.
Participants sat about 1 m apart, facing each other.

A monitor was placed behind each participant and aligned such that participants could shift their gaze between their partner's face and the monitor positioned next to their partner without moving their heads.
Participants could not see the content displayed on their own monitor while facing their partner.
At the beginning of each condition, participants received written instructions displayed on the monitor positioned in front of them (adjacent to their partner).
Depending on the condition, the monitors either displayed biosignal information or remained black.
During biosignal sharing, the relevant monitor displayed filtered ECG and skin conductance level (SCL) traces, along with numerical values for heart rate and SCL.
During the baseline periods, the participants turned around to watch the neutral video on their own monitors.

During biosignal-sharing conditions, physiological signals were streamed in real time using Lab Streaming Layer (Kothe et al., 2025) and visualized on the monitor via a custom Python interface implemented with PyQtGraph.

text.text: The incoming ECG and EDA signals were continuously buffered and displayed as scrolling traces over a 10-s rolling window.
For visualization purposes, signals were low-pass filtered using a zero-phase 4th-order Butterworth filter with a 20-Hz cutoff frequency.

text.text: In addition to these established instruments, we developed a General Experiment Questionnaire (GEQ) to capture beliefs, perceptions, and behaviors specific to the experimental context.

The GEQ included items assessing familiarity with biosignals (e.g., principles, analysis, and interpretation of ECG and EDA), confidence in recognizing biosignal features, and beliefs regarding the relationship between physiological signals and mental states.

Two versions were administered (see Supplementary Material): Version A (GEQ-A), completed prior to the experiment, assessed baseline familiarity, beliefs, and concerns; Version B (GEQ-B), completed after the experiment, probed changes related to the sharing and observation of biosignals and included items assessing subjective experiences during the interaction (e.g., gaze direction, attention allocation, and perceptions of the partner's attention).
Additional items measured affective responses, discomfort, and concerns related to biosignal sharing.

From GEQ-B, items 9-11 were combined into a composite score reflecting efforts to divert attention from face-to-face interaction in order to manage discomfort or feelings of overwhelm (Cronbach's alpha = 0.840).

GEQ-A items and GEQ-B items 1-11 were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (Strongly Disagree) to 6 (Strongly Agree), whereas GEQ-B items 12-15 were rated on a 7-point scale ranging from 0 (Not at all) to 6 (All the time).

text.text: Upon arrival at the laboratory, participants met for the first time and were informed about the experimental procedure.
After providing written informed consent, they were guided to the experimental room and seated in designated positions facing each other (see Section 2.2).

The experimenter introduced the biosignal acquisition devices and prepared the physiological measurement equipment, including ECG and EDA electrodes and the respiration belt, as detailed in Section 2.5.

Participants then completed the Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (SIAS), the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), the Inclusion of Other in the Self (IOS) scale, and the General Experiment Questionnaire Version A (GEQ-A).
During this period, electrode contacts and physiological signals were allowed to stabilize.
The experimenter continuously monitored signal quality and adjusted electrode or belt placement when necessary.
Participants subsequently received oral instructions describing the experimental setup and task.
They were instructed to look at each other or at their partner's biosignals if available, and to behave naturally and relax while refraining from any overt form of interaction (verbal or gestural).
They were also asked to minimize large movements, particularly of the arms and shoulders, and to avoid laughter, as these behaviors could introduce artifacts into the physiological recordings.
Participants then proceeded to the experimental conditions.
Condition-specific instructions were displayed on the relevant monitor prior to each block.
Before each experimental condition, participants watched a neutral baseline video.
Although breaks were permitted if needed, no dyad requested a break during the experiment.

Throughout the session, the experimenter continuously monitored the biosignal quality and, if necessary due to persistent artifacts in the recordings, paused the experiment to adjust the acquisition devices.
After the experiment, participants completed a second set of questionnaires: the IOS scale and the version B of the General Questionnaire.
During electrode removal, participants were debriefed and informally asked about their experience.
The entire session lasted approximately 80 minutes, including around 40 minutes for preparation, electrode placement, and questionnaires, and approximately 40 minutes for the experimental conditions.

During the experiment, we collected participants' ECG, EDA, and respiration signals using the BITalino PsychoBIT bundle (PLUX Wireless Biosignals S.A., Lisbon, Portugal) at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
ECG was acquired using three electrodes placed on both clavicles and the left iliac crest, following an Einthoven Lead II configuration.
EDA electrodes were placed on the distal phalanges of the left index and middle fingers, and a respiration belt was positioned around the ribcage between the 8 th and 10 th ribs.
Electrode contacts were allowed to stabilize for approximately 15 min before recording.
Sensor placement and acquisition procedures followed manufacturer recommendations and relevant literature (Boucsein, 2012; Prochazkova et al., 2022; van Dooren et al., 2012).

text.text: To examine participants' physiological states, we analyzed signal features reflecting parasympathetic and sympathetic activity.
From ECG recordings, we computed the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) of R-R intervals, an index of parasympathetic regulation.

From EDA recordings, we extracted the skin conductance level (SCL), the number of skin conductance responses (SCRs), and their mean amplitude, which index sympathetic activation (Boucsein, 2012; Pham et al., 2021).
text.formatted: From EDA recordings, we extracted the skin conductance level (SCL), the number of skin conductance responses (SCRs), and their mean amplitude, which index sympathetic activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Boucsein, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Pham et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Feature extraction was performed using NeuroKit2 (Makowski et al., 2021) and custom Python scripts.
text.formatted: Feature extraction was performed using NeuroKit2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Makowski et al., 2021)</ref> and custom Python scripts.

text.text: Signal features were computed over the full five-minute duration of each experimental condition.
Baseline values were calculated for each condition using the final three minutes of the preceding neutral video baseline.
To compute the RMSSD, the raw ECG signal was preprocessed and R peaks were detected to derive interbeat intervals (IBIs).
Preprocessing included highpass filtering at 0.5 Hz (5th-order Butterworth filter) to remove slow drifts, and notch filtering at 50 Hz to attenuate power-line interference.
The R peaks were detected using a custom algorithm based on a slidingwindow approach designed to identify high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) segments.
The algorithm compared signal power between two windows: a 60ms window capturing candidate R peaks and a 500-ms window estimating the surrounding noise.
A moving root-mean-square (RMS) standard deviation was computed, and regions exhibiting higher power values in the 60-ms window were flagged as potential peak segments.
Within each segment, the point of maximum amplitude was identified as an R peak.
A minimum inter-peak interval of 200 ms was enforced to exclude physiologically implausible detections.
This approach proved robust in moderately noisy recordings.
Heavily noisy segments were manually removed after visual inspection.
Concatenation of clean signal segments occasionally introduced spurious R-R intervals at segment boundaries.
To address this, IBIs shorter than 300 ms or longer than 1300 ms were removed based on physiological plausibility and visual inspection.
Additional outlier IBIs were identified and excluded using a threshold of 2.5 times the median absolute deviation (MAD), computed separately for each condition (Leys et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Additional outlier IBIs were identified and excluded using a threshold of 2.5 times the median absolute deviation (MAD), computed separately for each condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Leys et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The RMSSD was then computed from the remaining IBIs for each experimental condition.
The EDA signal was pre-processed by applying a 4th-order Butterworth lowpass filter with a cutoff frequency of 3 Hz and visually inspected for artifacts.
The signal was then decomposed into phasic and tonic components.

Portions of the signal fluctuating above 0.05 Hz were categorized as phasic EDA, representing skin conductance responses (SCRs), while portions fluctuating below 0.05 Hz were categorized as tonic EDA, or skin conductance level (SCL).

From the phasic component, we extracted the number of SCRs (EDA peaks) and their amplitude using the NeuroKit method; that is, local maxima in the signal were identified as peaks, and only those with amplitudes exceeding 10% of the maximum peak height were retained as SCR occurrences.
Statistical analyses were performed on the mean values of the physiological metrics of interest: RMSSD, SCL, the number of SCRs, and the mean amplitude of SCRs.
All physiological analyses followed a within-subjects design.
Metrics were compared across experimental conditions: Face-to-Face (F2F), Observing (O), Sharing (S), and Bidirectional Sharing (BS).
The unidirectional condition was split according to participant role (observing vs. sharing).
Physiological features were also correlated with psychometric questionnaire scores.
All statistical tests used an alpha level of 0.05, unless otherwise specified.
ANOVAs were performed using the Pingouin package (Vallat, 2018, v0.5.4), permutation t-tests with MNE Python (Gramfort et al., 2013), and Spearman correlation tests with SciPy.

All permutation tests were two-tailed and based on 5000 permutations.

text.text: We first assessed the reliability of the baseline periods by comparing the mean values of each physiological metric across the four baseline video-watching segments.
Mean values were submitted to a one-way repeated measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geisser correction, followed by pairwise permutation t-tests.
We then examined whether the experimental conditions induced changes in autonomic activity relative to their respective baselines.
For each condition, mean physiological metric values were compared to those of the immediately preceding baseline period using permutation t-tests.
To investigate the effects of biosignal sharing, physiological metrics were baseline-corrected by subtracting the mean value of the baseline period preceding each experimental condition.
Baseline-corrected values were then submitted to separate one-way repeated-measures ANOVAs with Greenhouse-Geisser correction for each metric, followed by pairwise permutation t-tests.
We evaluated experiment-induced changes in participants' perceptions and comfort levels with respect to the sharing and interpretation of physiological signals.
To this end, we compared responses from the General Experiment Questionnaire collected before (GEQ-A) and after (GEQ-B) the experiment.

Specifically, we examined changes in: belief in the link between physiological signals and internal states (1B-5A), confidence in inferring emotions from physiological signals (2B-6A), discomfort with sharing physiological signals (4B-7A), and concern about exposing internal states (6B-8A).
We also compared IOS scores collected before and after the experiment to assess changes in perceived interpersonal closeness.
All comparisons were performed using permutation t-tests.
To examine associations between physiological states and psychological traits, questionnaire scores and self-report items (summarized in Table 1) were correlated with physiological features.
text.formatted: To examine associations between physiological states and psychological traits, questionnaire scores and self-report items (summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>) were correlated with physiological features.

text.text: For each biosignal-sharing condition (Bidirectional Sharing, Observing, and Sharing), baseline-corrected physiological metrics were further normalized by subtracting the corresponding baseline-corrected values from the Face-to-Face condition.
These normalized values were then correlated with questionnaire scores and self-report items using Spearman's rank correlations.
For each metric and condition, 25 correlations were tested, and pvalues were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method.
These 25 items were also correlated with each other, applying the same false discovery rate correction procedure.

text.text: Our findings highlight that sharing physiological signals during social interaction modulates sympathetic arousal and can influence perceived interpersonal closeness.

Specifically, bidirectional biosignal sharing (BS) was associated with reduced skin conductance level (SCL) compared with face-to-face interaction without sharing (F2F) and both unidirectional sharing roles.

Similarly, the number of skin conductance responses (SCRs) was significantly reduced during bidirectional biosignal sharing (BS) compared with both face-to-face interaction without sharing (F2F) and the unidirectional sharing role (S).

Moreover, this reduction in arousal was functionally meaningful: greater reductions in SCRs during bidirectional sharing (relative to F2F) were associated with larger increases in perceived interpersonal closeness.
These results extend prior qualitative work by providing quantitative physiological evidence that the reciprocity of biosignal sharing is an important determinant of its psychophysiological impact.

The presence or perceived presence of an observer typically elicits heightened sympathetic arousal, self-awareness, and impression-management processes (Bond, 1982; Cottrell et al., 1968; Hamilton and Lind, 2016; Yoshie et al., 2016; Zajonc, 1965).

text.text: These effects are shaped by social comparison and they arise from efforts to appear competent or avoid disapproval, as well as by fluctuations in cognitive capacity due to the attentional conflict induced by the presence of others (Aiello and Douthitt, 2001; Guerin, 1993).

text.text: Such audience effects likely account for the general elevation in sympathetic activation observed across all interactive conditions in our study, relative to the baseline video-watching periods where mutual observation was not feasible.
Research on biosignal sharing suggests that making covert physiological information externally available may further amplify these audience effects.

Since physiological signals are involuntary and difficult to control, sharing them can feel like losing autonomy over what is revealed about one's internal states (Feijt et al., 2023; Slovák et al., 2012b).

text.text: In this context, unidirectional sharing configurations are often perceived as intrusive, potentially reinforcing audience effects.
Conversely, reciprocal sharing may mitigate such concerns, as mutual exposure restores a sense of fairness and shared vulnerability (Feijt et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Conversely, reciprocal sharing may mitigate such concerns, as mutual exposure restores a sense of fairness and shared vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Feijt et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This framework aligns with our main finding of reduced sympathetic arousal during bidirectional exchange, and with the observed association between lower sympathetic activation in BS (relative to F2F) and increased perceived interpersonal closeness.
Under this framework, one might expect unidirectional sharing to elicit stronger sympathetic activation than F2F interaction, given the heightened asymmetry of exposure.
However, our data did not support this pattern.
A plausible explanation is that the F2F condition, despite lacking biosignal sharing, is among the strongest possible evaluative potentials in day-to-day social interactions.
Indeed, participants informally reported during debriefing that the F2F condition was perceived as the most stressful and effortful part of the experiment.

Thus, the elevated arousal inherent to this social-interaction "baseline" could have created a ceiling effect, limiting the detectability of additional audience effects introduced by unidirectional sharing.
Beyond general audience effects, the reduction in arousal during bidirectional sharing may be influenced by shifts in visual attention.
Direct eye contact is a strong social cue that consistently increases sympathetic arousal (Helminen et al., 2011; Myllyneva and Hietanen, 2015).
text.formatted: Direct eye contact is a strong social cue that consistently increases sympathetic arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Helminen et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Myllyneva and Hietanen, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: During face-to-face and the unidirectional sharing role, participants lacked alternative visual anchors and were likely to sustain continuous gaze toward each other, maintaining elevated arousal.

In contrast, bidirectional sharing introduced an alternative visual element (the biosignal display), which could have intermittently diverted gaze and reduced the duration and frequency of mutual eye contact, thereby decreasing arousal.
Crucially, however, this reduction in arousal cannot be attributed solely to the screen acting as a visual distraction.
No comparable reduction was found in the observing-only condition, where participants also viewed the display of their partner's biosignals.
This observation challenges the purely attentional-diversion account.

Rather than attributing the observed effects solely to shifts in visual focus or mutual gaze, our findings suggest that attention-related processes may interact with the social context in which biosignals are shared.

However, because attention allocation was not measured objectively, further research is needed to clarify how gaze behavior and attentional deployment contribute to the biosignalsharing effects reported here (see Section 4.3).
Our correlational findings provide further insight into how perceived exposure and observation relate to participants' psychophysiological and subjective experiences during biosignal sharing.

Specifically, the number of SCRs during bidirectional sharing (relative to face-to-face interaction) was positively associated with how often participants felt their partner was looking at their biosignals, indicating that higher sympathetic activation co-occurred with a stronger subjective perception of being observed.

This association is consistent with prior accounts linking perceived monitoring to heightened self-awareness and evaluative concern, previously described as audience effects (Bond, 1982; Cottrell et al., 1968; Hamilton and Lind, 2016; Yoshie et al., 2016; Zajonc, 1965).

text.text: In addition, participants' exposure-related discomfort was positively associated with greater unease when their own biosignals were being viewed.
Importantly, this discomfort was paralleled by increased concern about causing discomfort when monitoring a partner's biosignals.
This pattern points to a reciprocal awareness of vulnerability, whereby concerns about being watched were mirrored by concerns about scrutinizing others.

Along similar lines, participants' perception of having their biosignals observed was positively associated with how much they reported looking at their partner's signals, suggesting mutual monitoring dynamics and attunement to the other person's behavior, rather than a purely unidirectional focus on exposure.
Furthermore, a stronger perceived sense of being observed was associated with smaller increases in perceived interpersonal closeness following the experiment.
Taken together, these associations suggest that heightened monitoring and self-focused awareness may co-occur with elevated sympathetic arousal, potentially hindering closeness formation.

This pattern aligns with prior work indicating that comfort with physiological transparency depends on perceived reciprocity, control, and contextual safety, rather than on access to physiological information per se (Feijt et al., 2023; Slovák et al., 2012b; Wikström et al., 2021).

text.text: Our results should be interpreted in light of some limitations.

First, regarding visual attention processes, our questionnaire items captured participants' subjective perceptions of observing the partner or their biosignals, and of having one's own biosignals observed, but did not objectively quantify visual attention.
Consequently, interpretations concerning the specific role of eye contact and attentional diversion (e.g., monitoring the biosignal display) warrant further investigation.
Future work should explicitly measure attention allocation using objective methods such as eye tracking, electrooculography, or electrophysiological indices of visual engagement (e.g., SSVEPs).

Combining such measures with analytic approaches, such as Granger causality or other directed connectivity estimators, could help elucidate the temporal interplay between attentional shifts and autonomic regulation, and clarify whether moment-to-moment gaze dynamics underlie the physiological effects observed during bidirectional sharing.
Second, the effects of biosignal sharing are likely shaped by the social context and relationship between interacting individuals.
Our sample consisted of strangers engaged in a minimal, nonverbal face-to-face interaction, a setting that may heighten social-evaluative awareness.
Prior work suggests that the meaning of biosignal sharing varies with relational closeness and situational framing (Feijt et al., 2023; Janssen, 2012; Slovák et al., 2012b; Stepanova et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Prior work suggests that the meaning of biosignal sharing varies with relational closeness and situational framing <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Feijt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Janssen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Slovák et al., 2012b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Stepanova et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should therefore examine how these dynamics unfold in more naturalistic interactions and across different social bonds (e.g., friends or romantic partners) and social contexts (e.g., cooperative vs. evaluative).
Third, our implementation displayed minimally pre-processed biosignals to isolate the fundamental effects of sharing.
However, interface design can strongly modulate social interpretation (Moge et al., 2022).
text.formatted: However, interface design can strongly modulate social interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Moge et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should systematically vary the modality, aesthetics, and framing of the biosignal display to understand how design choices might further shape psychophysiological responses.
Notably, we did not observe significant experimental or biosignal-sharing effects for the ECG-derived RMSSD metric.

Thus, while biosignal sharing modulated sympathetic arousal as indexed by EDA-derived measures, it did not produce detectable changes in parasympathetic activity as reflected by this standard HRV measure.

Previous evidence has suggested that HRV during first-time face-to-face encounters is often characterized by an initial drop that remains stable throughout the interaction, showing no statistical variation across different interaction contexts (Rudnicki et al., 2019).

text.text: Moreover, it has been suggested that standard HRV metrics may lack sufficient temporal resolution to capture the non-stationary cardiac dynamics characteristic of brief social or cognitive tasks (Candia-Rivera et al., 2025).

text.text: Future studies employing ECG feature estimators with higher time resolution may therefore provide more accurate insights into ongoing autonomic dynamics and the parasympathetic contributions during biosignal sharing.
Finally, while we focused on individual physiological responses, social interaction is inherently dyadic.
Interpersonal EDA interdependencies have been linked to shared attention, attunement, and social connection (Palumbo et al., 2017; Prochazkova et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Interpersonal EDA interdependencies have been linked to shared attention, attunement, and social connection <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Palumbo et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Prochazkova et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this work, future studies should examine how partners' physiological signals covary during biosignal sharing.

Investigating how autonomic coupling unfolds across different sharing configurations, and how it relates to objective measures of attentional deployment, may clarify whether biosignal sharing influences physiological interdependencies, and whether these interdependencies contribute to the changes in perceived closeness observed in our study.
Our study provides quantitative evidence that biosignal sharing influences both autonomic regulation and perceived interpersonal closeness.
Specifically, we show that bidirectional biosignal sharing significantly reduces sympathetic arousal relative to both face-to-face interaction without sharing and the unidirectional sharing role.

Importantly, this physiological attenuation was socially meaningful: participants exhibiting larger reductions in sympathetic activation also reported greater increases in perceived interpersonal closeness.
Our findings further point to an interplay between exposure, perceived scrutiny, and empathyrelated processes in shaping participants' experiences during biosignal sharing.

Together, these results highlight reciprocity as a key variable shaping the autonomic and relational impact of biosignal sharing and provide quantitatively grounded insights for the design of social computing systems and computermediated interactions.

Figure 1: Experimental setup and design.
(A) During the experimental conditions (left panel), pairs of participants sat facing each other while their electrocardiography (ECG) and electrodermal activity (EDA) were recorded simultaneously.
Participants could not see the display of their own signals while facing the partner.
Depending on the experimental condition, the monitor either remained black or displayed a real-time visualization of the partner's biosignals.
During baseline condition (right panel), participants sat back-to-back and watched a neutral video on their own monitor while ECG and EDA were measured.

(B) The experiment comprised four 5-min face-to-face blocks: (1) Face-to-Face without biosignal sharing (F2F), (2) Unidirectional Sharing (S), in which the participant shared their biosignals while the partner observed; (3) Unidirectional Observing (O), in which the participant observed the partner's biosignals without sharing, and (4) Bidirectional sharing (BS), in which both participants simultaneously shared and observed each other's biosignals.
During the sharing conditions, the display showed realtime ECG and skin conductance level traces along with numerical heart-rate and SCL values.
Each block was preceded by a baseline period.
Block order was counterbalanced across dyads.
